strengths: The core idea is original and well-articulated: casting multivariate EDAs over an autoregressive neural generator trained with a GRPO/PPO-KL objective, and enforcing order-invariance by sampling independent random generation and training permutations (dual uniform orders). The interpretation of this mechanism as an information-preserving analogue of structured dropout (Appendix E, including the analysis of the distribution of available conditioning contexts and the comparison with plain input dropout) is a genuine conceptual contribution.

The technical development is careful: the PPO derivation for this MDP (Appendix B) is correct, the extension to differing generation/training orders (Appendix C) is handled properly with a correct telescoping argument and a reasonable justification for importance ratios not sharing the same conditioning, and Lemma 1 establishes unbiasedness of the population-based surrogate estimator. The connection to the IGO/natural-gradient framework (Appendix G) grounds the rank-based advantage design.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for this area: 504 competing algorithms from Nevergrad plus PBIL, MIMIC, BOA and a one-flip Tabu baseline, three problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3), three instance sizes, multiple instance types, 100 independent runs per configuration, and t-tests at p=0.01. The claim that the method scales well (best or near-best on n=128 and n=256 while staying robust) is supported by Table 3 and the convergence curves.

Ablations are thorough and convincing: the four order-noise variants, the Learned-σ (Plackett-Luce) variant showing that learning an explicit order is counterproductive, dropout-replacement ablations (Figures 6-9), gray-box interaction-graph experiments (M.3), and sensitivity analyses of λ, β and network capacity (M.4-M.6). These directly support the paper's mechanistic claims about why dual random orders help.

Hyperparameters (Table 2), instance generation details, timing information, and experimental protocol are documented in sufficient detail for independent reproduction, and instance data is reported to be in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Scope of evaluation is limited to three synthetic benchmark families. No real-world black-box problems (e.g., expensive simulation, hardware configuration, drug design tasks) are evaluated, which limits the significance of the claim that the method is suited for 'expensive' black-box optimization.

The reproducibility statement is internally inconsistent and weak: Section 6 says source code 'will be published soon,' while Appendix K states the code is in the supplementary material. Code availability cannot be verified, which is a reproducibility risk for an algorithm with many implementation details (probability clipping, single-sample estimation of the training-order expectation, adaptive β, etc.).

The scalability of the architecture is not seriously addressed: one separate neural network per variable (with an m×n parameter matrix) plus population λ=10 and 50 training epochs per generation makes the approach computationally heavy; the paper only notes parameter sharing as future work, and largest experiments stop at n=256.

The convergence argument in Appendix D is heuristic: it assumes infinite population/capacity and treats the rank-based advantage as a stationary reward, providing intuition rather than a guarantee. There is no theoretical result connecting order-invariant training to actual optimization performance.

Known failure modes are acknowledged only in the appendix (e.g., failure to converge within budget on NK3 with K=8, non-best performance on n=64, stagnation on QUBO after ~3-4k evaluations), and there is no dedicated limitations discussion in the main text.
Several main-text figures (Figures 1, 2) are small with illegible axis labels and legend text, which hurts presentation; the key Table 3 with the headline results is relegated to an appendix.

Fairness of the large benchmark comparison relies on default hyperparameters for all 504 competitors; while a defensible black-box protocol, it may disadvantage methods that are known to need tuning, and the one-flip Tabu baseline beats the proposed method on many small instances, indicating the advantage is mainly in the mid-size regime.

strengths: The paper is technically thorough: the PPO/GRPO adaptation to the EDA setting is carefully derived (Appendices B–C), the unbiasedness of the population-based estimator is proven (Lemma 1, Appendix D), and the interpretation of random generation/training orders as information-preserving structural dropout is analyzed in depth (Appendix E), including a comparison with naive Bernoulli input dropout.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this area: the proposed method is benchmarked against ~504 algorithms from Nevergrad plus PBIL, MIMIC, BOA and one-flip Tabu search, over three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3), multiple sizes (n=64–256) and instance types, with 100 independent runs per configuration and two-sample t-tests (p<0.001) for significance.

Substantial ablation and sensitivity work: comparison of the four order-sampling variants, structural-dropout ablations, learned Plackett-Luce orders, known interaction-graph (gray-box) analysis, and sensitivity to population size, KL coefficient β, and network capacity (Appendices M, Figures 6–13).

Full hyperparameter tables, instance generation protocols and pseudocode are provided, supporting reproducibility of the experimental setup; the paper positions itself honestly within the IGO framework (Appendix G), giving a principled justification for rank-based advantages.
weaknesses: Evidence for the central claim (order-invariant training improves over fixed-order training) rests almost entirely on one instance distribution (pseudo-boolean NK, N=256, K=4) in Section 4.1; the observed gaps between variants are sometimes modest and no statistical tests are reported for this key comparison.

Evaluation is limited to synthetic benchmarks (QUBO, NK, NK3) with a 10,000-evaluation budget and n≤256; there are no real-world or application instances, and the claim that the method 'scales well with instance size' is only weakly supported by three sizes on synthetic problems.

The architecture dedicates an independent MLP to every variable (θ ∈ R^{n×m}), so parameters grow linearly with n; the authors only mention parameter sharing as future work, and there is no explicit limitations discussion of compute cost (~9 min/instance on GPU per run) or applicability to larger problems, whereas simple competitors like one-flip Tabu are nearly free computationally.

Results are mixed rather than dominant: on the smallest instances (n=64) the method is consistently not the best, and on the hardest NK3 instances (K=8) it fails to converge within budget; the abstract's claim of 'frequently achieves the best performance' is somewhat stronger than Table 3 warrants.

Novelty is incremental: the ingredients (NADE-style permutation ensembles [61], σ-GPT random-order training [41], PPO-KL/GRPO [51, 55], rank-based utilities from IGO [39]) are existing, and the contribution is primarily their combination in the EDA context; the theoretical development is competent but largely a transplantation of known results.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time: the Reproducibility Statement only promises that code 'will be published soon', and the supplementary material with the detailed result tables is referenced but its availability is uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: applying autoregressive neural generators to multivariate EDAs for discrete black-box optimization, avoiding the costly and brittle explicit DAG structure learning of classical EDAs (MIMIC, BOA).

The core idea is well motivated and articulated: random generation/training orders act as an information-preserving analogue of structural dropout, promoting order-invariance, population diversity, and hierarchical ('residual') dependency learning; the analysis in Appendix E (uniform permutation masks leading to a weighted MLE expansion over conditioning subsets) gives a plausible mechanistic account.

The methodology is carefully derived: the PPO/TRPO surrogate adapted to undiscounted terminal-reward EMDPs (Appendix B), the extension to decoupled generation vs. training orders (Appendix C), an unbiasedness lemma for the Monte-Carlo objective (Appendix D), a reasoned choice of KL-regularized (rather than clipped) PPO in the presence of varying masks (Appendix F, engaging with Hausknecht & Wagener's dropout/RL results), and an IGO connection (Appendix G).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and fair: ~500 Nevergrad algorithms plus PBIL, MIMIC, BOA, and Tabu, across QUBO, NK, and categorical NK3 at n ∈ {64, 128, 256}, 100 runs per distribution with statistical significance testing, and a fixed hyperparameter configuration across problems.

Thorough ablations: order variants ((δ,δ'), (δ,σ'), (σ,δ'), (σ,σ'), learned Plackett-Luce orders), structural dropout vs. permutations (M.1/M.2), known interaction graph (M.3), and sensitivity to λ, β, and network capacity (M.4–M.6). The finding that learned order distributions underperform random ones is an interesting, useful negative result.
weaknesses: The theoretical treatment of the decoupled generation/training order objective is heuristic. Equation (8) trains with masks σ'(x)<k that differ from the sampling masks σ(x)<k, so the importance-sampling ratio is not a proper ratio of densities of the same conditional; the paper acknowledges the resulting bias but only argues informally that it is 'acceptable' when policies are close, and never quantifies the bias or studies its effect empirically (e.g., by measuring the KL between the two conditioning distributions).

Originality is moderate: the ingredients (autoregressive factorizations, random orderings à la NADE/σ-GPTs, GRPO-style rank-based advantages, KL-regularized PPO) are each established; the contribution is their combination and adaptation to the EDA setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. The claim 'no prior work has applied autoregressive to EDA' should be softened given neural/meta-model surrogates in optimization are well explored.

The theoretical analysis is thin relative to its framing: Lemma 1 is a straightforward exchangeability argument, and the 'convergence' discussion in Appendix D (as t→∞ the population degenerates; with infinite λ the limit is the global optimum) is informal and does not constitute a convergence guarantee.

Evaluation is limited to synthetic benchmarks (QUBO/PUBO, NK, NK3) up to n=256. No real-world combinatorial instances (e.g., Max-Cut, Ising, scheduling) are tested, which limits evidence for the practical significance claims. On the hardest instances (K=8) the method fails to converge within budget, and on small instances (n=64) it is not the best, so the 'frequently best' claim holds mainly in a specific regime.

Off-policy/policy-ratio concerns interact with the tiny population (λ=10) and 50 epochs of reuse: rank-based advantages with a population of 10 give a very noisy learning signal, and the paper does not analyze variance of the resulting gradient estimates, despite emphasizing sample efficiency.

Statistical methodology is coarse: pairwise t-tests against the 'best other competitor' across ~505 algorithms with no multiple-comparison correction; rankings based on mean score over 100 runs on only 10 instances per distribution may overstate reliability.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the code 'will be published soon' rather than being included, although hyperparameters, instance generators, and algorithm pseudo-code are well documented.

Presentation needs polish: numerous typos ('solide lines', 'On possible explanation', 'derivated', 'telescop'), the key quantitative results (Table 3) are relegated to the appendix while the main text relies on a single comparison figure, and Figure 1/2 are hard to read at the reproduced scale.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of ideas: adapting any-order/permutation-invariant autoregressive generative models (in the spirit of σ-GPTs/NADE ensembles) as the probabilistic model of a multivariate EDA, and connecting this to policy-gradient RL with GRPO-style rank-based advantages grounded in the IGO framework.

The derivation of PPO updates when generation and training orders differ (Section 3.3, Appendices B–D) is careful, and the paper honestly identifies the resulting off-policy approximation and support condition rather than hiding it.

Unusually thorough ablation and sensitivity analysis: the four (σ/δ) order variants are compared, structural dropout vs. permutation masking is analyzed analytically and empirically, and the paper includes critic-based, Gibbs-sampling, parameter-sharing, and curriculum variants, plus hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, β, E, network depth).

Very broad empirical evaluation: ~500 Nevergrad algorithms plus PBIL/MIMIC/BOA across QUBO, NK, NK3 (n up to 1024), and a real NAS-Bench-101 application, with 100 runs per configuration and significance tests; code and instances are supplied for reproducibility.

The paper is transparent about weaknesses of the method: it documents slow early convergence, poor performance on NK3 with K=8, the need for parameter sharing at large scale, and the higher cost of critic/Gibbs variants.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely a synthesis of known components (any-order autoregressive models, PPO-KL/GRPO, rank-based IGO advantages) rather than a new algorithmic principle; the theoretical analysis (Appendix D) is limited to unbiasedness of the surrogate and informal infinite-data/capacity asymptotics, so the central 'order-invariance improves sample efficiency' mechanism is supported mostly empirically, not theoretically.

The importance-sampling ratios in Eq. (8) use different masks in numerator and denominator; the authors argue the support condition holds, but the resulting bias away from on-policy PPO guarantees is only argued informally and could be examined more rigorously.

Computational cost is significant: ~5 minutes GPU (or 11.5 minutes CPU) per instance of size 128 for a 10,000-evaluation budget, i.e., the neural overhead per evaluation is large; the paper argues this is acceptable for expensive objectives but does not compare against equally resourced neural baselines for discrete BO/CO.

Baseline coverage has gaps: no comparison with recent neural generative optimizers, discrete Bayesian optimization (e.g., BOCS-style or COMBO), or modern learned-construction methods for CO, which would clarify where the method genuinely sits in the landscape.

Abstract claims ('frequently achieves the best performance and consistently avoids catastrophic failures') are somewhat stronger than the evidence: the method is dominated at small budgets and fails to converge on rugged NK3 instances (K=8), which the paper itself documents in Appendices P and M.

Presentation has noticeable flaws: minor typos ('solide', 'dentified', 'splitted'), and the main text leans heavily on the very long appendix (roughly two-thirds of the manuscript), making key results and the convergence discussion harder to follow in the main body.

strengths: The core idea—training an order-invariant autoregressive generative model as the probabilistic model of an EDA, with random generation orders acting as information-preserving structural dropout—is well motivated and cleanly separated from existing solution-space symmetries (e.g., POMO, Sym-NCO).

The theoretical scaffolding is unusually careful for this area: the TRPO/PPO-style derivation is adapted to the undiscounted, terminal-reward EDA setting (Appendix B), extended to differing generation/training orders (Appendix C), and an unbiasedness lemma for the population-rank advantage estimator is proved (Appendix D). The connection to IGO and the analysis of permutation-induced masking versus standard input dropout (Appendix E, Figure 4) provide genuine insight into why the mechanism works.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 500+ competitor algorithms from Nevergrad on QUBO, NK, and NK3 instances at multiple sizes, plus NAS-Bench-101, with 100 independent runs per distribution, statistical significance testing, and full pseudocode, complexity analysis, and source code in the supplementary material.

Extensive ablations (variants (δ,δ)/(δ,σ)/(σ,δ)/(σ,σ), Gibbs-sampling baseline, critic-based advantages, shared-parameter variant, curriculum adaptation, sensitivity to λ, β, E, and network depth) give a reasonably complete picture of what drives performance.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated relative to the evidence. The method only 'frequently achieves the best performance' on larger instances (n=128, 256) after the full 10,000-evaluation budget (Table 4). At n=64, and especially at a 1,000-evaluation budget (Table 5), it is dominated—often ranking in the hundreds out of 504—and it fails to converge on NK3 instances with K=8. The abstract's claim of 'consistently avoids catastrophic failures' is contradicted by the authors' own admission that the method 'fails to converge within the allocated budget' on the hardest instance distributions.

The headline 'best performance without any change to hyperparameters' is undermined by the appendix material: strong results required a curriculum variant with a hand-tuned ρ=0.993, a separate 'Fast-(σ,σ)-RL-EDA' for low budgets, and tuned advantage-scaling coefficients (α) for the critic variant. The main-text algorithm is effectively one point in a large, sensitivity-heavy design space (Figures 13–16 show nontrivial sensitivity to λ, β, E).

Compute cost is a significant and underweighted limitation: ~11.5 min CPU / 5 min GPU for a single n=128 instance with 10,000 evaluations (Table 3), versus ~78s for the strongest simple competitor (CMApara). The comparison protocol budgets competitors by wall-clock time while the proposed method is evaluated by function-evaluation budget, which flatters the neural method. This asymmetry should be treated more prominently.

The theoretical contributions are largely incremental: Appendix B is a standard PPO derivation in new notation; the unbiasedness lemma (D.1) follows directly from linearity of expectation and exchangeability; and the 'convergence' discussion in Appendix D is informal (a hand-wavy λ→∞ degeneracy argument rather than a real guarantee). The importance-sampling argument when masks differ between numerator and denominator (Eq. 30) is asserted to be well-behaved ('the behavior distribution is still non zero everywhere...') without any variance analysis, yet this off-policy/mismatched-mask regime is precisely where the method departs from standard PPO.

Originality is moderate: the paper combines known components—order-invariant autoregressive modeling (σ-GPT, NADE ensembles), GRPO, PPO-KL, and rank-based utilities from IGO—applied to the EDA loop. The synthesis is competent but the individual ingredients and even the 'random orderings as regularization' insight have close precedents the paper itself acknowledges (Hausknecht & Wagener 2022).

Presentation quality is uneven: dense and error-prone notation (σ(x)<k versus xσ<k), duplicated derivation steps (Eqs. 39–40), typos ('solide lines', 'sore', 'latsly', 'perform' for 'performs'), and tables/figures whose legibility matters but is hard to verify (e.g., Figure 2 axes). Key results (Table 4) are relegated to an appendix, making the main paper's empirical claims hard to assess without the supplement.

The comparison against prior EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA) uses only default hyperparameters from a third-party implementation, which is a weak baseline for the direct ancestors of this work; the strongest evidence for the method's value comes from beating broadly engineered Nevergrad baselines, where the time-budget asymmetry again complicates interpretation.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: the proposed (σ,σ)-RL-EDA is benchmarked against 500+ Nevergrad algorithms plus classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA) across QUBO, NK, and NK3 instance distributions at multiple sizes, with 100 independent runs per configuration and statistical significance tests (t-test, p<0.001) reported in Tables 4-6.

Extensive and convincing ablations: the decomposition of the method into (δ,δ), (δ,σ), (σ,δ), (σ,σ), and learned-order (Plackett-Luce) variants cleanly isolates the contribution of random generation vs. training orders; the supplementary comparison with structural dropout (App. N), a Gibbs-sampling order-free variant (App. S), a critic-based advantage variant (App. Q), and a parameter-sharing variant for large instances (App. R) shows the design choices are empirically justified rather than arbitrary.

Theoretical grounding is present and mostly sound: the PPO/TRPO-style derivation (App. B-C) correctly telescopes advantages across generation orders, the unbiasedness of the Monte-Carlo estimator (Lemma D.1) is proven, and the connection to the IGO framework (App. G) provides a principled interpretation of the rank-based, scale-invariant advantage (Eq. 5), which is a meaningful adaptation of GRPO to the black-box optimization setting.

The analysis of random training orders as information-preserving structural dropout (App. E, including the mask distribution analysis and Figure 4) is an interesting conceptual contribution that explains *why* the method works, not just that it does.
Strong reproducibility: source code, generated instances, complete per-distribution results, hyperparameter tables, wall-clock timings (Table 3), and an LLM-usage declaration are all provided.

The paper is honest about limitations: it openly reports that the method is dominated at small budgets (Table 5), fails on rugged K=8 instances within budget, underperforms at n=64 with the default configuration, and proposes (and evaluates) a curriculum variant (Fast-(σ,σ)-RL-EDA) that addresses the small-budget regime.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest relative to the paper's framing: the formal results are an unbiasedness lemma and an informal asymptotic argument in the infinite-data/infinite-capacity regime; there is no convergence or sample-complexity guarantee for the actual finite-λ algorithm, so the claim of incorporating varying orders into PPO 'in a theoretically principled way' is only partially substantiated.

Practical cost-effectiveness is a concern: the method requires a GPU and minutes (up to ~50 minutes CPU at n=256) per instance and converges slowly, so simple, fast baselines like DiscreteLenglerOnePlusOne or NLOPT variants dominate it at low budgets and on small instances (n=64). The headline advantage is concentrated on larger instances (n=128, 256) at the full 10,000-evaluation budget, which narrows the practical applicability claim.

Originality is more compositional than fundamental: any-order autoregressive modeling (σ-GPTs, NADE order ensembles), GRPO, and rank-based advantages from IGO/CMA-ES utility theory are each well established; the novelty lies in their combination for EDAs and the empirical demonstration, which is valuable but incremental from an ML-methodology standpoint.

Evaluation is limited to pseudo-Boolean and small-categorical benchmarks (QUBO, NK/NK3, NAS-Bench-101); no problems with constraints, larger categorical domains, or non-synthetic structure beyond NAS-Bench-101 are considered, and the poor behavior on the hardest rugged instances (K=8) is noted but not resolved.

Presentation issues reduce readability: the notation is heavy (dual roles of σ, masks σ(x)<k vs. σ'(x)<k), and there are numerous typos and grammatical errors ('solide lines', 'telescop', 'accross', 'foresight', 'connexion') that suggest insufficient proofreading; the derivations in the main text could be compressed.

The wall-clock time comparison (Table 3) shows (σ,σ)-RL-EDA is 5-20x slower than CMApara on CPU; while the authors argue objective-call budget is the right criterion, the practical relevance of the speed gap for time-limited settings is not fully discussed.
